summary:
Canarias stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 on legal gender recognition and LGTBI rights, and adds a regional layer of its own: Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 on non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognition of trans persons' rights (BOE-A-2014-11995), which gives a trans visitor a region-specific statutory basis against discriminatory treatment.

The community has permitted trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 Spanish autonomous communities to do so before the national statute of 28 February 2023 took effect. A visitor to Canarias therefore encounters self-identification as the operative regional practice, predating and now aligned with the national route.

Canarias is also listed among the Spanish communities banning conversion therapies, so the practice is prohibited within the region's own competence as well as under the national framework.

On relationship recognition, the Canary Islands created their same-sex couple registry in 2003, a regional instrument that predates the nationwide same-sex marriage regime in force since 2005.
tangentialFactors:
Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally as LGBT tourist destinations, which shapes the environment a trans visitor will meet: established venues, visible community presence and a hospitality sector accustomed to LGBT clientele on those two islands.

The regional pattern is one of several in Spain. Canarias belongs to the group of 14 autonomous communities that had opened gender self-declaration before the national statute, and to the group that bans conversion therapies, so its protections are not an outlier but part of a wider sub-national layer that varies across the country.
localsOnly:
Residents of Canarias can invoke Ley 8/2014 directly as a regional non-discrimination guarantee covering gender identity, alongside the protections of the national organic law.

Self-declaration of legal gender has been available in the community since 2021, so residents have had a working regional procedure for several years rather than only since the 2023 national statute.

The regional ban on conversion therapies binds practitioners operating within Canarias, and the same-sex couple registry of 2003 remains part of the community's own relationship-recognition machinery.
outOfScopeNotes:
No region-specific enforcement data, court decisions or reported incidents of anti-trans violence in Canarias were identified in the source inventory; the assessment rests on the statutory layer alone.

Whether the regional conversion-therapy ban carries administrative or disciplinary penalties, and which body applies them, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The current text and any amendments to Ley 8/2014 since its publication in 2014 are not confirmed by the available sources, nor is the present operation of the 2003 couple registry.
